1:
Keil and Delitzsch open the chapter by comparing it with another. The incidents of Isaac's life collected here resemble in many respects certain events in the life of Abraham, yet their distinctive peculiarities form a true picture of dealings perfectly suited to the character of this patriarch. Famine drove Isaac out of Canaan as it had driven his father; Abraham went to Egypt, where his wife was exposed to a danger from which only God's direct interposition could rescue her; Isaac intended the same journey, but at Gerar was instructed to stay, since as the seed to whom the land was promised he was not to leave it. Gill fixes the famine in Canaan, as the Targum of Jonathan expresses it. Ellicott supplies the geography that makes the detour intelligible: Isaac was then living at the well Lahai-Roi, and though its site is unknown it lay too far south for Gerar to fall on his direct road into Egypt.

Calvin measures the trial. Isaac was tried by nearly the same kind of temptation through which his father had twice passed, and the assault was severe and violent. The condition in which God willed to place his servants, as strangers and pilgrims in the land he had promised to give them, seemed hard enough; more intolerable still that he scarcely suffered them to exist in this wandering and changeable life, but almost consumed them with hunger. Who would not say that God had forgotten himself, when he did not supply his own children however sparingly, with food? But God so tried the holy fathers that we might be taught by their example not to be effeminate and cowardly under temptations. He adds a note, that there were two seasons of dearth in Abraham's time and Moses alludes only to the one whose remembrance was most recent.

Henry reads the famine as providence testing what the word had taught. Isaac had been trained up in a believing dependence upon the divine grant of Canaan to him and his heirs, and now the promised land will not find him bread: what shall he think of the promise? Yet Isaac still cleaves to the covenant, and the less valuable Canaan seems in itself the better he is taught to value it — as a token of God's everlasting kindness and as a type of heaven's everlasting blessedness. The intrinsic worth of God's promises cannot be lessened in a believer's eye by any cross providences.

Henry carries that reading forward over the direction which follows, and finds its point in three famines compared. There was one in Jacob's days and God bade him go down into Egypt, one in Isaac's and God bade him not, one in Abraham's and God left him to his liberty, directing him neither way; some ground the difference on the characters of the three men, Abraham being of such high attainments that all places were alike to him, Isaac very good but not cut out for hardship, Jacob inured to difficulties and therefore sent where the trial of his faith might be to praise and honour and glory. Thus God proportions his people's trials to their strength. Those who must live by faith, Henry adds, have need often to review the promises they are to live upon, especially when called to any act of suffering or self-denial.

Clarke cannot date the famine, except that it appears to have fallen after Abraham's death, and he raises the question the chapter never settles: whether this Abimelech and this Phichol are the men of the earlier narrative or their sons and descendants. Calvin decides it — not the Abimelech of the twenty-first chapter but perhaps his descendant, the name being probably common to the kings of Gerar as Pharaoh was to those of Egypt, and meaning My father the king, since kings ought to be the fathers of their country.
2:
Why Isaac was stopped short of Egypt is the question they press. Calvin takes the oracle as the reason he went to Gerar rather than to a country perhaps more convenient: he was withheld by a heavenly word, so that a free choice was not left him. Why then prohibit the son what the father had been suffered to do? Moses gives no reason, but Calvin conjectures the journey would have been more dangerous to Isaac. God could have endued him with the power of his Spirit, as he had Abraham, so that the delicacies of Egypt should not corrupt him by their allurements; but since he governs his people with such moderation that he does not correct all their faults at once, he assists their infirmities and anticipates with suitable remedies the evils that might ensnare them. Knowing more infirmity in Isaac, he was unwilling to expose him, being faithful and not suffering his own to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear.

Clarke reaches the same conclusion from character. Abraham had taken refuge in Egypt, so probably Isaac was preparing to go likewise, and God, foreseeing trials there which might prove fatal to his peace or to his piety, warns him off. The reasons are not assigned, and probably Isaac himself was never informed of them; while a man acknowledges God in all his ways he will direct his steps, though he may not choose to give the reasons of his providence. Abraham might go safely to Egypt and Isaac might not, for in firmness and decision of character there was a wide difference between them. Gill keeps to the plain sense of the command, that Isaac was to stay within Canaan — Gerar, though of the Philistines, being a part of it — Abraham having been careful of the same thing for his son while he lived.

What the appearing itself was worth Ellicott states by counting. Only once besides does Jehovah manifest himself to Isaac, and sixty years had passed since the revelations at the mount of offering; excepting to Abraham, it was only at rare and distant intervals that God spake to the patriarchs. The greater part of their lives was spent under the same ordinary Providence which governs us now, and on special occasions God confirmed their faith in a way no longer necessary, now that the whole counsel of God has been made known to us.

On the terms of the promise Calvin guards against a misreading. Moses does not mean that Abraham's obedience was the reason the promise was ratified; what God freely bestows is sometimes ascribed to the faithful beyond their desert, that knowing their intention approved they may devote themselves the more ardently, and the father's obedience is commended to stimulate the son to imitate it. Though laws, statutes and rites had not yet been written, Moses uses those terms to show how sedulously Abraham regulated his life by the will of God alone, abstaining from every heathen impurity and pursuing the straight course of holiness without turning to the right hand or the left. Wesley draws the practical edge: those only shall have the benefit of God's covenant with their parents who tread the steps of their obedience. Clarke turns to the words themselves, the Targum reading my Word, and the charge coming from the verb to keep, its ordinances being of two kinds — such as promote moral improvement and piety, and such as were typical of the promised seed. Gill limits the multiplied seed chiefly to the line of Jacob, from whom sprang twelve patriarchs, and refers the obedience above all to the offering of the son. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead instead, to the sister told of at Gerar as she had been in Egypt, and to a protection managed very differently this time.
6:
Henry sets the scene as obedience walking straight into temptation. Isaac had now laid aside all thoughts of going to Egypt and, in obedience to the heavenly vision, sets up his staff in Gerar; yet there he enters the same temptation his good father had been once and again surprised and overcome by. Because his wife was handsome he fancied the Philistines would find some way to take him off, that one of them might marry her; so she must pass for his sister. It is an unaccountable thing, Henry says — and Wesley repeats him almost word for word — that both these great and good men should be guilty of so strange a piece of dissimulation, by which they so much exposed both their own and their wives' reputation.

Two lessons he draws from the fall. Very good men have sometimes been guilty of very great faults and follies: let those therefore that stand take heed lest they fall, and those that have fallen not despair of being helped up again. And there is an aptness in us to imitate even the weaknesses of those we value; we have need therefore to keep our foot, lest, while we aim to tread in the steps of good men, we sometimes tread in their by-steps. The falls of those gone before us are so many rocks on which others have split, and the recording of them is like placing buoys to save future mariners.

Calvin weighs the same imitation and makes it the aggravation rather than the excuse. Isaac was led by his father's example, that being instructed by the similarity of circumstances he might be associated with him in faith; but on this very point he ought rather to have avoided than imitated his father's fault, since he well remembered that his mother's chastity had twice been in great danger, and that though she was wonderfully rescued both she and her husband paid the penalty of their distrust. His negligence is inexcusable, striking against the same stone. Two charges lie against him: that to preserve his life he resorted to an evasion not far removed from a lie, and that in absolving his wife from conjugal fidelity he exposed her to prostitution. Whence appears how great is the propensity of our nature to distrust.

Clarke asks whether the father was to blame for the son's ignorance. Did Abraham never mention the circumstance to Isaac? Probably not, being justly ashamed of the only blot in his character; and the son, not forewarned, was not armed against the temptation. From that he turns to advice for parents: it may not be well in general to tell children of former failings, yet cases occur where a candid acknowledgment with suitable counsel may prevent the evil being repeated, done with caution lest the advice itself serve as an incentive, since Paul had not known lust if the law had not said, Thou shalt not covet.

Whether the words were a lie at all Clarke settles against Isaac. Abraham could say of Sarah, She is my sister, and speak literally; Isaac could not, Rebekah being only his cousin. He meant the Gerarites to understand him strictly and to suspect nothing, and the proper definition of a lie is any word spoken with the intention to deceive. Ellicott marks how differently the two episodes ran: here the people, not the king, make the inquiry, and though she was fair to look upon no annoyance followed the denial; when the king does detect them there are no presents, no marks of respect to Rebekah and no friendship, and only after long quarrels, which drive Isaac far from Gerar, is peace at last made. Gill reads the inquiry itself as neither idle nor innocent, arising from the prevalence of lust, yet under some restraint, since adultery was detestable to them though fornication was made no account of.
8:
How long the deception lasted Gill takes from the idiom: the Hebrew says days were prolonged to him there, and days are sometimes put for years, so perhaps years. What the king saw Clarke will not define beyond its force — whatever the precise meaning of the word, it implies liberties taken and freedom used which were not lawful but between man and wife. On the king himself Wesley repeats what is by now settled, that this is the common name of the Philistine kings as Caesar was of the Roman emperors. Ellicott counts eighty years since Abraham's sojourn and agrees the same man can hardly still be reigning, yet notes that king and people alike maintain the good character previously deserved; the Philistines at this period were only a feeble colony of strangers, kept in restraint by a sense of their own weakness, and only later received the accession of strength that made them formidable enemies of Israel.

Calvin finds the mercy in the manner of the rescue. Truly admirable is the kind forbearance of God, who not only condescended to pardon the twofold fault of his servant but stretched out his hand and, by a speedy remedy, wonderfully averted the evil Isaac would have brought upon himself. God did not suffer what twice befell Abraham, that his wife should be torn from his bosom, but stirred up a heathen king to correct his folly mildly. Yet the faithful, though they may confidently hope to find God gentle and propitious if they fall, must beware of self-security: the holy woman who was then the only mother of the Church on earth was exempted from dishonour by a special privilege.

From the king's judgment Calvin infers Isaac's character and his own age's decline. We may conjecture how holy and pure the conduct of Isaac had been, on whom not even a suspicion of evil could fall; for why does Abimelech not condemn him as guilty of fornication, since some crime might well be concealed where a man obtruded the name of sister and tacitly denied her to be his wife? His religion and the integrity of his life availed to defend his character — by which we are taught so to cultivate righteousness that men may not suspect anything wicked or dishonourable of us, nothing more completely vindicating us from every mark of infamy than a life passed in modesty and temperance. The chastity of that age is further proved in this, that Abimelech took a familiar gesture between the two as evidence of their marriage. Now, Calvin ends, licentiousness has so broken through all bounds that husbands are compelled to hear in silence of the dissolute conduct of their wives.

The reproof and the edict close the episode. Gill hears the king asking why Isaac should entertain such jealousies of them as bad men, and expose them to the temptation of iniquity. Clarke thinks Abimelech may have had some knowledge of God's intentions concerning Abraham's family, that it must be kept free from impure and alien mixtures, so that had his people taken Rebekah the divine judgment might have fallen on the land; he calls him a good and holy man who considered adultery a grievous crime, and notes that death was its punishment among Canaanites, Philistines and Hebrews alike. Calvin reads the censure as discipline: God did not chastise Isaac as he deserved, but that the rebuke might produce the deeper shame he constituted a heathen his master and reprover, and it ought to have wounded the holy man deeply that his offence was obnoxious to the judgment even of the blind. The edict itself he takes for a special privilege, since it is not customary to avenge every injury so rigidly; and he asks what inclined the king to prefer a stranger to his own people, unless some portion of the divine majesty shone forth in him.
12:
Gill sets the sowing after the settlement, in the land of Gerar, once the king had ordered his servants to do Isaac no hurt; Clarke reads the same sequence as cause, that being now perfectly free from the fear of evil he betook himself to agricultural and pastoral pursuits and had God's especial blessing in them. Henry fastens on the timing, and Wesley after him: there is an emphasis on the year, for it was that same year when there was a famine in the land, and while others scarcely reaped at all he reaped thus plentifully — my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied. Henry adds an observation for the encouragement of poor tenants who occupy other people's lands and are honest and industrious, that Isaac had no land of his own but took land of the Philistines and sowed it, and God blessed him with a great increase.

What the hundredfold was they measure carefully. Clarke reports the phrase as literally a hundredfold of barley, which is how the Septuagint renders it, and thinks such a crop of that grain was perhaps a rare occurrence in Gerar, though the words may be taken generally for a very great increase, as our Lord uses them in the parable of the sower. Ellicott says the Hebrew is a hundred measures, the word being unknown elsewhere, and that the Septuagint and Syriac read a hundred of barley with measures understood; Herodotus mentions two and even three hundredfold as possible in Babylonia, but our Lord seems to give one hundredfold as the extreme of productiveness in Palestine, so that such a return would be rare and extraordinary.

Ellicott also sees a stage of life changing. When Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba it showed he regarded the place as a permanent residence, worth adorning; Isaac and Jacob took a further step toward settled life when they began to cultivate plots of ground. At first Isaac did no more than the Bedaween do now, who often sow a piece of land, wait till the crop is ripe, and then resume their roving habits, permanently to till the soil being with them a mark of inferiority. The famine had driven him from Beersheba and had probably cost him much of his cattle and many even of his people, leaving him no match for the Philistines of Gerar; this large harvest recouped his losses and made him a prosperous man again.

Calvin presses an objection the narrative invites. How could Isaac sow at all, when God had commanded him to be a stranger all his life? Some suppose he had bought a field, but the context corrects that error: we find soon afterwards that he was not delayed by having land to sell when he had to remove his effects elsewhere; purchasing land was contrary to his peculiar vocation and to God's command, and Moses would not have passed over so notable an offence; and since express mention is immediately made of a tent, we may infer that wherever he came he would dwell in the precarious condition of a stranger. He sowed, therefore, in a hired field. Though he had not a foot of land in his own possession, it behoved him as a good householder to prepare food for his family, and perhaps hunger quickened his care and industry to provide against the future — yet he received as a divine favour the abundance he had acquired by his own labour, as the psalm says that the Lord abundantly supplies his people while they sleep.
13:
Clarke hears the greatness in the sound of the Hebrew, which repeats one root three times — and the man was great, and he went, going on, and was great, until that he was exceeding great. How simple is this language, he says, and yet how forcible. Gill takes the growth in substance as well as in honour among men, and counts the wealth in sheep, oxen, asses and camels, in which the riches of those times chiefly lay. Possessions so extensive needed many hands, he adds, some servants born in the house and others bought with money. Ellicott presses the word behind that phrase: the margin reads husbandry, and literally it means making employment, answering to our word business — so the common rendering gives the sense, but we see besides that Isaac kept his people all actively employed.

Calvin draws from the envy a rule about prosperity. The blessings of God which pertain to this present earthly life are never pure and perfect, but mixed with some troubles, lest quiet and indulgence should render us negligent; therefore let us all learn not too ardently to desire great wealth. If the rich are harassed, let them know they are roused by the Lord lest they fall fast asleep in the midst of their pleasures; and let the poor take this consolation, that it is no light good to live free from envy, tumults and strifes. He so attempers the favour he shows his children in this world, Calvin adds, that he stirs them up as with sharp goads to the consideration of a celestial life.

On the stopped wells they are of one mind about the offence. Clarke notes that in such countries a good well was a great acquisition, so that in predatory wars either party would fill them to distress the enemy; here the act was most unprincipled, since the Philistines had pledged themselves to Abraham by a solemn oath not to injure each other in this very respect. Ellicott observes that in the East the digger of a well is reckoned a public benefactor, and supposes they stopped Abraham's because they counted an alien's possession an intrusion on their own rights; envious at his rapid increase they meant to drive him away, and no expedient could be more effectual than denying water to his cattle. Calvin calls it the extreme of cruelty, not only to defraud a stranger but to take what his own father's labour had won; and he thinks it no slight trial that water, the common property of all animals, should be denied the holy patriarch.

Of the dismissal Clarke makes the first recorded instance of what the Greeks called ostracism, the banishing of a man whose riches the people envied, and quotes Bacon's saying that public envy is an ostracism which eclipseth men when they grow too great. He doubts the usual rendering, since Isaac can hardly have been mightier than the king of whole tribes, and would translate it thou hast obtained much wealth among us, and my people are envious of thee. Calvin will not decide whether the king spoke as a friend or from an alienated mind, but takes from it that the most eminent fall under the suspicion of the common people, and infers how much more desirable a moderate condition often is. Gill admires the going: Isaac departed at once, peaceably, though to his own loss, taking neither to argument nor to arms. Keil and Delitzsch fix the retreat on the map, in the undulating land of Gerar through which the torrent from the town runs down from the south-east; and Ellicott explains the word rendered valley, a narrow defile down which a summer stream flows, in whose bed water can generally be found by digging. Isaac hoped he was now far enough from the city for the enmity to cease, and in that he was mistaken.
18:
Clarke opens with a textual point: for in the days of Abraham, Houbigant would read the servants of Abraham, a reading supported by the Samaritan, Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate, and probably the true one. Calvin explains why the old names went back on the old wells. Isaac gave no new ones but restored his father's, that by this memorial the ancient possession might be renewed; only later violence compelled him to change them, that he might by some monument make manifest the injury and reprove the Philistines for it. In calling one well Esek and another Sitnah he denies that the inhabitants held by right, or by any honest title, what they had seized as enemies or robbers.

How hard the straits were Calvin measures before he praises the patience. The holy man was so hated by his neighbours as to be driven to a retreat destitute of water, and no habitation is so troublesome as one that suffers scarcity of it; while his cattle and his servants, who were like a little army, made a supply the more necessary. That this last necessity did not instigate him to seek revenge is a proof of singular forbearance, since we know that lighter injuries will often rack the patience even of humane and moderate men. Nor was it weakness: he could not have undertaken a regular war, but as Abraham had armed four hundred servants, Isaac too had domestics enough to repel any force his neighbours brought.

Why the wells had been left stopped since Abraham's day Calvin reads as a verdict on the inhabitants. Their own country would have been the better for them, yet they chose to lose the advantage rather than have Abraham for a neighbour, and by filling them in they did, in a sense, intercept his way, lest such a convenience should draw him there. It was a custom among the ancients, when they wished to cut a man off from the society of men, to interdict him from water and fire; and this is what the Philistines did.

Of the three wells the notes run from philology to praise. Clarke renders the second phrase a well of living waters, the oriental expression for a spring in both Testaments, where an unfailing spring is an emblem of the graces and influences of the Spirit of God. Gill sets the first quarrel on the border, which is why it was disputable whose the water was, and has Isaac remove further from their boundary to cut off all pretence for the future. Wesley glosses Esek as contention and Rehoboth as enlargements, room enough, and draws the moral that those who follow peace shall sooner or later find peace, and those who study to be quiet seldom fail of being so. Clarke says never did any man more implicitly follow the command Resist not evil: whenever Isaac found his work likely to breed strife he gave place, choosing to suffer wrong rather than have his peace disturbed, and so overcame evil with good.

Henry sees the same lesson in the two names that failed. Contention and Hatred show the nature of worldly things, that they are make-bates and occasions of strife, and show too the lot of the most peaceable, who avoid striving and yet cannot avoid being striven with; and what a mercy it is to have plenty of water, and to have it without striving for it — the more common the mercy the more reason to be thankful. Calvin finds the patience proved at the third well rather than the first: when Isaac, freed at last from these troubles, so placidly returns thanks to God and celebrates his goodness, he shows that in the midst of trials he had kept a composed and tranquil mind. Keil and Delitzsch look on to Beersheba, where Abraham had spent long, and where the promises would be renewed by night.
23:
Gill has him return, the famine being over, to the place where he and his father had formerly lived. Calvin notes that Moses does not explain the cause of the removal, and supposes the Philistines never ceased to annoy him, so that the holy man, worn out by their malice, withdrew further off; he judges Isaac was sorrowful and anxious, for God appeared to him on the very first night after he arrived. That is the constant pattern: whenever Moses relates that God appeared to Abraham, he shows the man tormented with cares or borne down by fatigue, the hand of God being stretched out as his necessity required. Clarke says the same from the circumstances: Isaac needed especial encouragement when outraged by the Philistines, and returning where his noble father had lately died, the memory of his wrongs and his loss could not fail to afflict him.

Calvin weighs the oracle against the well and finds it heavier. In the tranquil enjoyment of the water Isaac acknowledged the favour God had shown him; but one word of God weighs more with the faithful than the accumulated mass of all good things, and we cannot doubt he received this promise more joyfully than if a thousand rivers of nectar had flowed to him. Whence we learn, while giving each of God's other gifts its proper honour, still always to give the palm to that proof of his paternal love which he grants us in his word. Food, clothing, health and peace afford us a taste of the divine goodness; but when he addresses us familiarly and declares himself our Father, then indeed he refreshes us to satiety. Wesley draws the plain comfort from it, that those may remove with confidence who are sure of God's presence with them wherever they go.

What a vision was for, Calvin explains. It was to convince Isaac that it was God with whom he had to deal, for a bare voice would have had less energy; visions were a kind of symbol of the divine presence. Should any object that such evidence was not sure, since Satan often deceives by similar manifestations, being as it were the ape of God, the answer is that a clear mark was engraven on the visions of God; and since Satan can only delude us in the dark, God exempts his children from that danger by illuminating their eyes with the brightness of his countenance. Yet God did not fully manifest his glory, but assumed a form suited to the measure of their capacities, so that Moses does not mean God was seen in his true greatness, but as Isaac was able to bear the sight. Nor was the appearance a mute spectre: the word followed, and its preface — I am the God of Abraham thy father — renews all the promises before given, that Isaac might not sever the present oracle from the former ones.

Of the altar Clarke says only that Isaac would have a place for worship as well as one to dwell in, and Gill that Abraham had planted a grove there before and probably built an altar too, now perhaps not standing. Calvin takes it for public worship, since inward invocation requires no altar and no special choice of place; but because religion ought to maintain a testimony before men, Isaac by erecting one professes himself a worshipper of the true and only God and separates himself from the polluted rites of the heathen — and he built it not for himself alone but for his whole household. He thinks it remarkable besides that a place already named from a well should oblige Isaac to dig for water again, and suspects the whole region had conspired to expel him by thirst, this well of Sheba too having been fraudulently stopped. Keil and Delitzsch look on from here to the treaty that follows.
26:
Why the king should come at all they answer from fear and policy. Gill supposes Abimelech was told that Isaac, settled at Beersheba, was still increasing in family and substance, and dreaded that he might resent his expulsion, and the herdmen's usage at the wells, and turn his riches and power against him. Ellicott sets the visit in a wider frame: the Philistines were themselves an alien race, and an alliance between Isaac and Ishmael and others of the Semitic stock might end in their expulsion; Abraham too had been confederate with the Amorites and friendly with the Hittites, who might aid his son. Isaac's return was therefore a serious matter, and the king, uncertain of his purpose, determined to offer peace and propose a renewal of the old covenant; matters had come to a crisis, and Abimelech must decide whether there was to be peace or war.

Calvin reads the same approach as evidence of a hand behind it. The Lord followed Isaac with the favour he had shown his father, and it was no common blessing that Abimelech should voluntarily seek his friendship, the neighbours who had harassed him being now afraid of him. There is not the least doubt the king was led by a secret divine impulse: if he was afraid, why not resort to some other remedy, or send for Isaac and command him with authority? But God had so forcibly impressed his mind that he forgot his regal pride and sought peace with a man who was neither covetous, nor warlike, nor furnished with a great army. Thus we may learn that the minds of men are in the hand of God, so that he can not only incline to gentleness those who before were swelling with fury, but humble them by terror as often as he pleases.

Over the names in the company Clarke and Ellicott hesitate together. Clarke thinks it likelier that Abimelech was a general name of the Gerarite kings and Phichol a name of office than that Abraham's two men were still living. For Ahuzzath he reports that the Targum makes it not a name but a company, so that the two came with a company of their friends, while the Septuagint calls him Ochozath the paranymph, who conducts the bride to the bridegroom's house — from which, if that could be trusted, one might infer this king to be the son of Abraham's friend, lately married, bringing the confidant to whom his spouse had been entrusted. Ellicott allows the same doubt, and says that if it be a name the rendering should be Ahuzzath his friend, his confidential adviser and privy counsellor.

Isaac's question they take for prudence rather than resentment. Gill hears him asking what the visit can mean, since it cannot come from affection; Clarke holds him justified, because if the Philistines did not injure him themselves they had connived at their servants doing it. Henry makes it a rule: in settling friendships there is need of the wisdom of the serpent as well as the innocence of the dove, and it is no transgression of the law of meekness plainly to signify our perception of injuries received, and to stand on our guard with those who have acted unfairly — though he sets against it the reason the visit came at all, that when a man's ways please the Lord he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him, kings' hearts being in his hand to turn as he pleases. Calvin agrees that it is lawful for the faithful to complain of their enemies, in order if possible to recall them from their purpose and restrain their frauds and injustice; for liberty is not inconsistent with patience, and God does not require of his own that they silently digest every injury, but only that they restrain their minds and hands from revenge.
28:
What the Philistines had seen Gill spells out: not only the fruitfulness of the land Isaac sowed while among them, and the increase of his family, flocks and herds, but the same blessing following him after he was gone, in the valley of Gerar and now at Beersheba. Calvin takes their words for proof that they sought the compact in good faith, since they acknowledge God's favour towards him; they had need to purge that suspicion, presenting themselves so courteously to a man they had lately opposed without reason. And the confession carries instruction. Profane men, in calling one whose affairs prosper the blessed of the Lord, bear testimony that God is the author of all good things and that from him alone flows all prosperity — so that base indeed is our ingratitude if, when God acts kindly, we pass by his benefits with closed eyes. They reckon the friendship of one whom God favours desirable, there being no holier commendation than the love of God.

That they should still be afraid of an inoffensive man Calvin finds the stranger part. They ought to have concluded from the favour God had shown him that he was just, and no danger to them; but because they form their estimate of him from their own conduct, they distrust his probity too. Such perturbation commonly agitates unbelievers, so that they are inconsistent with themselves, tossed between conflicting sentiments and having nothing fixed; for those principles of right judgment which spring up in their breasts are soon smothered by depraved affections.

Of the terms themselves the notes are short and the reading of them long. Clarke has them propose a covenant binding both and ratified in the most solemn manner; Gill hears in the request that Isaac do them no hurt a fear for persons and properties, kingdom and subjects alike. Calvin says an accusing conscience urges them to hold him closely bound, for they knew he might rightfully avenge what he had suffered; yet they dissemble on that point and even boast of their own kindnesses. The king's humanity had indeed been remarkable at first, when he not only entertained Isaac but treated him with peculiar honour — only he by no means continued so to the end. It accords with the common custom of men to disguise their faults by whatever colour they can invent; but if we have committed an offence it rather becomes us ingenuously to confess it than, by denying it, to wound more deeply those we have injured.

Isaac's forbearance Calvin makes the model. Having pierced their consciences sufficiently, he presses them no further, for strangers are not to be treated as domestics, and if they take no profit they are to be left to the judgment of God; and though he extorts no just confession, lest he seem to cherish hostility he does not refuse to strike a covenant. Thus we learn that those who have estranged themselves are not to be repelled when they offer themselves again: if we are commanded to follow after peace even when it flies from us, far less should we be repulsive when enemies voluntarily seek reconciliation, especially where there is hope of amendment, though true repentance may not yet appear. On the closing words Calvin declines the usual gloss that they are mere flattery, and reads them as an argument: Isaac had complained of being expelled through envy, and they answer that no grief need remain, since God had treated him so exactly according to his own wish — as if to say, grant that we failed in hospitality, yet the blessing of God suffices to obliterate the memory of that time. Wesley reads them the same way, that Isaac may be persuaded to overlook the injuries offered him, since those whom God blesses can afford to forgive, their worst enemy being unable to do them real hurt.
30:
Gill has Isaac make a feast like a king, for a king and his grandees, treating them generously according to their dignity and his own substance; Clarke supposes it was made on the sacrifice offered at the striking of the covenant, a common custom. Of the early rising Gill gives a reason from the business in hand: Abimelech and his friends rose to return home and Isaac to take his leave, but both also to make the covenant in form and confirm it by oath, and the morning was the fitter time, when the mind is free and composed, as so solemn a transaction should be performed with the utmost seriousness. Clarke gives a reason from the men themselves, that early rising was general among the primitive inhabitants of the world, and contributed greatly to their health and longevity.

Calvin uses the swearing to settle a question about oaths. Isaac does not hesitate to swear, partly that the Philistines may be the more easily appeased and partly that he may not be suspected; and this is the legitimate method of swearing, when men mutually bind themselves to peace. A simple promise ought to have sufficed; but since dissimulation and inconstancy make men distrustful of each other, the Lord grants them the use of his name, that this more holy confirmation may be added to our covenants — and he does not only permit it, he commands us to swear as often as necessity requires. Meanwhile we must beware lest his name be profaned by swearing rashly.

That the water came the same day Calvin will not let pass as a trifle. It appears from the account that the waters were not found in a moment of time; and if it be asked whence a supply was got for the cattle and the household meanwhile, he does not doubt Isaac either bought it, or was compelled to go some distance to find one from whom he might obtain it by entreaty. Ellicott leaves one point open which the ground itself keeps open: since there are two wells at Beersheba, it is uncertain whether this was Abraham's, re-opened by Isaac, or a new one altogether.

On the name they divide over which sense of an ambiguous word is meant. Gill reports Jerome's reading, that Sheba signifies fulness, as though the well were named from the abundance of water in it, but prefers to take it for an oath, so called from the oath just sworn — the two circumstances, the swearing and the finding, having met on one day. Clarke thinks it the same well that bore the name in Abraham's time, which the Philistines had filled and Isaac's servants reopened, and notes that the old name comes back with an added letter which extends its meaning, so that it now signifies not merely an oath or fulness but satisfaction and abundance; the name of the place had been given a hundred years before, but was probably abolished along with the well, and restored when Isaac restored the well. Calvin argues the same continuity from the word's ambiguity: those are mistaken who take this for any other name than the one Abraham first gave, for Abraham alluded to the covenant he struck with the king of Gerar, and Isaac, recalling that ancient memorial, joins to it the covenant in which he had himself now engaged. Ellicott observes that there was as yet no city there, one being first mentioned at the conquest under Joshua, and takes the closing phrase for a note added by Ezra and the Great Synagogue after the return from Babylon: its meaning is that whereas Abraham's name for the place had been forgotten while it lay desolate, this remarkable coincidence of the water being found again just as the covenant was confirmed so impressed the people that the title of Beersheba never again passed into oblivion.
34:
The age is the first thing noticed, and both who notice it read it alike. Gill observes that Esau was forty, the age his father had been when he married; Ellicott makes the coincidence exact, Esau being precisely the age Isaac had reached sixty years before when he married Rebekah. There the likeness ends. By thus intermarrying with idolaters, Ellicott says, Esau violated the great principle Abraham had laid down for his own son's marriage, forfeited his birthright thereby, and — such marriages being illegal — is even called a fornicator in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Henry weighs which part of the act was the folly. Some think it lay in marrying two wives together, for which perhaps he is called a fornicator; but rather in marrying Canaanites, strangers to the blessing of Abraham and subject to the curse of Noah, for which he is called profane, since he intimated that he neither desired the blessing nor dreaded the curse of God. Clarke suspects a calculation underneath: very likely the wives were daughters of Hittite chiefs, and by such a union Esau sought to strengthen his secular power and influence.

The grief to the parents Henry sets out in three counts. It grieved them that he married without asking, or at least without taking, their advice and consent — and see whose steps those children tread in who either contemn or contradict their parents in disposing of themselves. It grieved them that he married the daughters of Hittites, who had no religion among them; for Isaac remembered his own father's care concerning him, that he should by no means marry a Canaanite. And it should seem the wives themselves were provoking in their conduct towards Isaac and Rebekah — so that those children have little reason to expect the blessing of God who do that which is a grief of mind to their good parents.

Calvin asks why Moses should record these marriages at all, and answers that they were a kind of prelude of Esau's rejection: mingling with the inhabitants of the land from whom the holy race of Abraham was separated, he contracted affinities by which he became entangled. That the daughters-in-law proved grievous to Isaac and Rebekah he ascribes to the wonderful counsel of God, lest the parents should grow by degrees favourable to that reprobate people; for it was not lawful to bind in marriage those whom God had designed to be perpetual enemies. On the two wives together he is briefer: polygamy had so far prevailed that the custom, though vicious, had acquired the force of law, so that it is no surprise a man addicted to the flesh indulged his appetite. Wesley states the fault in a line, that Esau married Canaanites, strangers to the blessing of Abraham and subject to the curse of Noah.

Ellicott lingers over the names and gets history out of them. They are remarkable, he says, as showing that the Hittites spoke a Semitic tongue: Judith is the feminine form of Judah and means praised; Bashemath, the fragrant, was borne also by a daughter of Solomon; and Elon, oak-grove, was the name of a judge. Beeri can scarcely have been the father's original name, since it means well-finder, and was probably earned by his skill in discovering water — though the name occurs again in the genealogy of Hosea. He notes too that the wives are listed differently in the later genealogy of Esau, where a fourth wife from Seir takes the place of Judith, and that Esau afterwards partially repented, taking a daughter of Ishmael as a third wife. Because this conduct prepares the mind for his final rejection and the loss of the birthright, he judges that these two verses would stand more rightly at the head of the following chapter, and observes that the Jews arrange them as a separate section.
35:
Whether the bitterness came from the marriage or from the women is the one question the verse raises, and Gill and Clarke divide over it. Gill says the marriage itself was a trouble to them, it being contrary to their will that any of their children should marry with the Canaanites, and those the worst sort of them, the Hittites — Abraham having made it his own care that Isaac should not marry among them, and having laid a strict injunction on his servant not to take a wife for his son from that quarter, an example meant to be followed in later times and one Esau very likely knew. Clarke draws the line the other way: it was not the marriage, improper as that was, but the persons, who by their perverse and evil ways brought bitterness into the hearts of Isaac and Rebekah.

On the character of the women themselves the two come back together, and both lean on the same authorities. Gill finds them disagreeable on all accounts, partly by reason of their religion, being idolaters, and partly by reason of their temper and behaviour, being proud, haughty and disobedient, as all three Targums intimate. Clarke cites two of the same, the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel and that of Jerusalem, which say the wives were addicted to idol worship and rebelled against the instruction of Isaac and Rebekah alike and would not hearken to it. From Canaanites, he adds, a different conduct could not reasonably be expected: Esau was far from being spiritual, and his wives were wholly carnal.

Clarke closes the chapter by looking back over it, and the comparison he draws is not in Isaac's favour. The same reflections suggested by Abraham's conduct in denying his wife in Egypt and at Gerar apply to Isaac's, but Isaac's case was much the less excusable of the two, since Abraham told no falsity but only, through fear, suppressed a part of the truth. Against that he sets what the chapter has shown of God's dealing: a good man has a right to expect God's blessing upon his honest industry, for Isaac sowed and received a hundredfold and had possession of flocks, because the Lord blessed him. Worldly men, if they pray at all, ask only what they shall eat and drink and wherewithal they shall be clothed; most truly religious people run to the opposite extreme, forgetting the body and asking only for the soul — yet there are things requisite and necessary for the body as well as for the soul, and they too are only at God's disposal. Keil and Delitzsch let the verse stand as it is written, without comment.
